specs.anchorText: What you want is an estimator that ignores outliers entirely. Statistics has one ready: the median.

The bouncer gently points to the middle, average-looking gray character and ushers it through the door labeled-free entrance, while politely holding up a hand to stop one wildly over-the-top glowing bright-white character at the very end of the line who is trying to barge in. The bright outlier looks comically eager but is simply not chosen. Mood is calm and orderly, not mean. The style should be friendly and approachable, like a comic strip or an XKCD-inspired infographic, with expressive characters and minimal visual clutter. Suitable for a technical textbook. No text or lettering in the image. The humor is gentle: the loud outlier never gets picked, the sensible middle value walks right in. Keep the composition simple and focused on one clear visual metaphor of sorting and selecting the middle while the extreme is left out.
specs.alt: A calm cartoon bouncer lines up five pixel-characters in order of brightness and waves the sensible middle-gray one through the door, while politely stopping an over-bright glowing outlier at the end of the line from entering. The scene illustrates the median filter selecting the middle of a sorted window so a salt-and-pepper outlier is never chosen, unlike an average that would be dragged toward it.
specs.caption: The median filter just picks the sensible middle of the line, so a single screaming-bright outlier never gets in; an average, by contrast, lets the loud one drag the whole result toward itself.

specs.anchorText: Unsharp masking redistributes contrast that the sensor already captured; it cannot resurrect detail the optics never delivered.

specs.alt: A cartoon detective inspects a blurry photo through a magnifying glass; the magnified view gains bold outlines and glowing edge halos so it looks crisper, yet the underlying shape is just as fuzzy, and a thought bubble shows the truly missing detail marked only with a question mark. specs.caption: Sharpening just exaggerates the contrast already on file; it cannot invent detail the lens never recorded, which is exactly why dramatically enhanced license plates belong in fiction, not in court.

specs.caption: At the image border the kernel runs out of real pixels and has to make some up; whether it paints them flat gray, repeats the edge, or mirrors it decides whether you get a clean result or a dark vignette and false edges.
